On section 3,
This allows the company to raise on securities $40,000 a mile instead of $25,000, which it formerly had authority to raise.

This line passes through an old settled country, and the right of way through this country costs so much more than it would through a new country, where the right of way practically costs nothing, we thought it proper to allow them to raise $40,000 per mile.

The company shall not construct or operate its railway along any highway, street or other public place without first obtaining the consent expressed by by-law of the municipality having jurisdiction over said highway, street or other public place, and upon terms to he agreed upon with such municipality.

I object to that amendment. I think the Canadian Northern railway should be placed under the same jurisdiction and under the same terms generally as the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway. These are the three great trunk lines of the country, and I think they should all be under the terms of the General Railway Act. The Canadian Pacific railway has its main charter and a great many branch lines charters; the Grand Trunk railway has its main charter and the Grand Trunk Pacific branch lines charter, and so has the Canadian Northern railway, all now under the General Railway Act, which provides that they should only go across or along a highway on obtaining the consent and approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners. It is true that in the last three or four years we have inserted in

new -charters the clause which has been moved by my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), that is, that they -shall not go along or across a highway without the consent of the municipality, and upon terms to be agreed upon with the municipality. Now this is creating a discrimination against the Canadian Northern railway, if this term is imposed on this charter, and I think we would do well to leave it under the Railway Act where the other great railway corporations are. It might be that some municipality through which it passes would have power absolutely to block the road by refusing its consent. I think we can trust the matter in the hands of the Board of Railway Commissioners, -and for that reason this amendment should not be added to the Bill. If it were a new charter and a new company, then this argument might apply. But this road was largely constructed before we ever placed this clause in Bills which apply to trunk lines.

I have no objection, so far as I am concerned, to leaving it to the Board of Railway Commissioners. It is a clause we have usually inserted in all the Bills that now come before the committee. I think it is a perfectly legitimate clause. The fact that it is not in the Grand Trunk railway or the Canadian Northern railway charters does not make any difference to me. If they came up for a charter now, so far as I am concerned, 1 would advocate putting it in their charter, and on the same principle as I advocate this. This railway proposes to pass through all the older settled sections of Ontario, and I do not think that any railway should have a right, even with the consent of the Railway Board, to go along a road in a municipality without its consent. It is not crossing a highway, it is merely going along a highway. The clause inserted there does not say crossing a highway, it simply says going along a highway.

I do not think that amendment should be withdrawn. We have been in the habit of putting it in all other Bills we have given of late years. Because the Canadian Northern Railway Company had its original charter before we commenced this practice is to me n-o strong reason why we should now treat it differently from the way we have treated others when giving them charters to build railways. It applies to a section of country where it is equally desirable that the municipal corporation should have some control, and something to say as to what shall be done with their highways, as it would with reference to a new corporation to which we give that power. Consequently there is just as strong a reason why it should be in this Bill as in any other Bill we give, and I see no reason why the Canadian Northern railway should be exempt from it any more than any other company
who are asking for incorporation. I think it is a very proper one. I would be inclined to control them in that way, but when they propose to go along the highways or public places, the municipality should have something to say as to where the railway shall go and upon what terms.

I do not think the clause a bad one, but I think it ought to be in the Railway Act-, and not in particular charters. This is not a new charter, but application for the renewal of an old one, which did not contain any such clause. I think, therefore it would be a hardship to insert that in the old charter. When a charter was before us a few weeks ago for a Grand Trunk Pacific branch, we did not insert any such provision.

There is another objection which I think is serious against this proposed amendment. Under the municipal Act of Ontario, I understand, a municipality can only give a railway company a franchise for a period of 20 or 25 years. This would consequently limit the right of this road to run over a municipal roadway for that short period of time. Bonds issued upon a railway, usually extend for 30 or 40 years. Anybody who knows anything of this question, will know that it is impossible for a railway company to issue bonds over a piece of road on which it has no right to run except during a period of 25 years. For that reason, since this is an old charter, it would be just as well to let it through; but, in any new charter, a clause such as this, might seem to be advisable.
I think what my hon. friend refers to are corporations or railways, such as electric roads, which come under the Provincial, and not under the Dominion Act.

I was not aware that there was any such provision in the Ontario Municipal Act, and I am inclined to think that my hon. friend may not, be exactly correct. That would be a serious objection, but I have never understood the Ontario Act to apply in that way. I want to say a word with regard to a suggestion made by the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), that this is a clause which should be in the General Railway Act. That is an objection which comes to us whenever we propose to insert something new in the charter of any railway company seeking incorporation; but we have almost invariably decided that until these things are in some general Act, we should put them into the special Acts we enact. Parliament has deemed it wise to insert such provisions in special Acts and to continue doing so until such time as they are incorporated in a general Act. With re-

gard to this Bill, the hon. member says that if this were a new charter he would favour this amendment. I cannot appreciate the distinction. We are asked to give the company power to build these new branches, and are giving it new rights just as we would in the case of a new charter. We are not seeking to deprive the. company of any of the rights it possesses under its original charter; but when it asks the right to construct other lines, we are only doing our duty if we impose such conditions as we think ought to apply to the case of any new railway.

I am perfectly willing to withdraw the amendment, if the committee thinks it is better that it should go into the general railway Act.
Amendment withdrawn, Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

That in the opinion of this House, the present system of operating terminal and transfer elevators is detrimental to the interests of the Western grain producers, and that the government should take immediate steps to operate terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur, and the transfer elevators between those terminals and the Atlantic seaboard.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in submitting this important motion to the House, I do not think I need make any apology. I know that when questions of this kind, affecting Western Canada, have been brought before this House, some hon. members from eastern Canada have been inclined to regard them as of no interest to themselves. But, Sir, if there is any one question that is of national importance to this country today, it is the question of elevators. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition the other clay referred to the splendid progress that is being made by Canada, as evidenced by the great growth in population and importance of the great cities of eastern Canada. If Montreal to-day has a population of over half a million and Toronto boasts of a population nearly as great, I think I can justly claim that 75 per cent of the advancement made by these large eastern cities is due to the progress and development of the three prairie provinces. I think it would surprise very many members of this House to have accurate statistics of the trade which has come to eastern Canada because of that development. That western country is overrun with commercial travellers representing all branches of trade and industry in this country, and I believe the great manufacturing concerns of the country admit that their trade and prosperity during the last ten years has been largely due to the development of the Northwest. If that is a fact, and I believe it is, why should not eastern Canada be deeply interested in the great question of elevators? It is true, my motion has reference especially to what are called terminal and transfer elevators; but to my mind there is a strong connecting link between all the elevators which are utilized in the handling of the grain from the time it leaves the farmer's wagon until it reaches its ultimate market. This subject has been debated before in this House. A few days ago the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin) brought up a motion on the subject, and although it did not contain all that it should, liis speech did. I read the speech of the hon. gentleman, and I do not think he will take any exception to the statement that his general conclusion was that the only way in which we could properly control these terminal and transfer

elevators was by the system which I propose to-day, of government operation. I want to say that I do not approach this subject with any partisan motive. If there is any subject upon which the western members can agree, it is this one of elevators, which is closely allied to the great question of transportation.
Now, we have in this country what may be termed three classes of elevators. First, we have the line elevators which are scattered over the three prairie provinces wherever there is a line of railway. We have the Canadian Pacific railway, the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Pacific, and in some places the Great Northern. I am of opinion that eastern Canada would be surprised to know the number of elevators scattered over these three provinces and the amount of capital that is invested in this elevator business. I repeat, there is no question of such vital importance to the national prosperity of this country today as the elevator question. I think I would not be far astray in saying that there are some 2,000 of these line elevators scattered over the three prairie provinces. The Canadian Pacific Railway has over 1,100, the Canadian Northern some 460, the Grand Trunk Pacific some 111, and the Great Northern some 24. This is only a rough estimate, but it is within the mark.
These line elevators are the links between the farmer's wagons and the railways. They are not absolutely necessary. We have what we call loading platforms, and it was somewhat of a surprise to me to find that during the last year some 15,000,000 bushels of wheat were loaded from these platforms. But I am still of th? opinion that the elevator is the most legitimiate and the most convenient method of handling our grain from the farmer's wagon to the railway. A great deal of the difficulty suffered in the western provinces during the early years has no doubt been remedied, and there is not to-day so much fault to find with these line elevators, yet there remains a problem in that connection which we have been striving for some time to solve. We had a very important meeting which was attended by the Prime Ministers of the three western provinces for the purpose of arriving at some solution but apparently they were not able to accomplish any result, and the great cry in western Canada a few years ago, at any rate, was for government ownership of these line elevators. The province of Manitoba adopted that principle. The farmers and producers of that province, whether Liberal or Tory, made up their minds that government ownership was the only way in which these line elevators could be operated satisfactorily. I had something to do with the last contest in Manitoba, and I make this statement, that I never on any platform heard any speaker,
no
whether Liberal or Conservative, take the stand that the government operation of line elevators was not in the best interests of the country. The only argument used by our Liberal friends was this, that the government 'was not sincere, and that on the night of the election all government building and operation in this connection would cease. That, however, has not been the case. I mention that fact simply to shew that both parties were then unanimously in favour of that system. As regards Saskatchewan, I am not as familiar with what that province has done as some of my hon. friends opposite, but, from what I have read in the press, it has not exactly adopted government operation of line elevators but appointed a commission to investigate, and that commission reported, as I understand, that a company shall be formed, the officers of which should be the executives of the Grain Growers' Association of the province of Saskatchewan, and that the government should guarantee the bonds to the extent of 85 per cent of the money required to build, the company furnishing the other 15 per cent, and the bonds to be redeemed in 20 years. I also understand that the government was to undertake the financing of the concern, but I do not know as to how that part of the money invested -was to be repaid.
This question was debated by the Farmers and Grain Growers' association of Saskatchewan last week, and although there was some diversity of opinion, and although some two or three years ago nothing would satisfy any of the farmers except government ownership, it seems that the Saskatchewan grain growers, in the proportion of about six to one, decided to accept the report of the commission, and no doubt that report will be ratified by the local legislature, and the system recommended by the commission will be the way in which the elevators in that province will be operated. I presume that would be called government co-operation.
As regards Alberta, I am not aware that any steps have been taken to establish any such system of elevators. Although there may be diversity of opinion as to how these line -elevators are to be operated, I do not think there is any diversity of opinion among the grain growers as to how the terminal elevators should be operated in the best interests of the producers. Other methods have been tried -but we have all come to the conclusion that the warehouse men must not have an interest in the grain. As to the ownership, I do not know that it makes very much difference who owns these elevators, but it does make a tremendous difference to the producers who shall operate them. I am not one of those who desire any cleavage between the east and the west. I believe

that the east needs the west, and that the west appreciates to a very great extent the east. I believe in our working together and in encouraging interprovincial trade as much as possible. Thereiore, as I have already said, this is not particularly a western question. There is, of course, a difference in the industrial development of the west and the east. The city of Winnipeg is becoming quite a manufacturing centre, but the three prairie provinces are essentially given to grain growing and cattle raising. In the east and in British Columbia you have your lumber, your fruit growing and manufactures, and a great many other industries from which you can receive a revenue, but that is not the case in the prairie provinces. Our industries being limited in these provinces as they are, it is the more necessary that we should find the means of deriving the very best financial results from the pursuit of the two great industries I have mentioned.
I may be asked: Why has the west so recently taken such a stand? There are different reasons. Conditions have changed somewhat in the west. The raising of wheat has become more expensive. One reason for this is that help, both indoors and outdoors, is more expensive. Another question that might be referred to in this connection, but which I shall not deal with to-day, is the transportation question-transportation has certainly become more expensive: freight rates, storage and loading. In fact, the business of the farmer to-day is to give close and intelligent attention to all parts of his industry that enter into the production and marketing of grain from the time he plants the seed until he receives his remuneration in the markets of the world. Until recently the farmers were willing to jog along in the old way, to be the victims, figuratively speaking, of the lightning rod exploiter and the shoddy-cloth peddler. But within the last two or three years a change has come over the farmer. What has brought it about? Nothing short of co-operation. The other branches of industry sought the aid of co-operation much earlier than the farmer did. The manufacturers of this country have found it advantageous-and I am not finding fault with them for it; there is nobody more pleased than I api that our manufacturers are making money. But, perhaps, some of them are making too much money. I know a manufacturer in the city of Toronto who lives in a palace that, I think, cost more than all the buildings in a whole township in my constituency. It is questionable whether that is exactly what we want. Millionaires may be good, but I agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), who, if I understood him right, recently suggested that it is not particularly the business of Mr. SCHAFFNER.
this country to build up millionaires, but it is the business of this country to secure the greatest good for the greatest number of people. Our farmers are beginning to wake up; they are taking a leaf out of the book of the manufacturer and railways and are trying what co-operation will do. We have had for years, for instance, the Patrons of Industry and other societies for the benefit of the farming population, but the old excuse always came up, 'The farmers cannot stick together.' Thinking people reached a condition of mind in which they were unwilling to ally themselves with these associations, because of the want of stability and stick-to-it-iveness on the part of the farmer. But I thoroughly believe that that is all changed. We had a very good evidence of that here not long ago, when seven or eight hundred of these western farmers came down-and not with the money of Jira Hill either, but paying their own expenses-and this Chamber rang with the enthusiasm and earnestness of these people, as, I believe, it never rang before. These people are in earnest. Some will say-I have had it said to me: These tarmeTS want the earth; they want too much. Perhaps they are asking for a little too much; perhaps I am asking a little too much to-day. But did never the manufacturers come to this House and ask for too much? Did never the railways come to this hall and ask for too much? They certainly have. And I assure you the farmers to-day are ready and willing, although they may be asking a good deal, to accept what is in their best interest and in the interest of the country. And that is what I stand for here to-day. I say the farmers have begun to think for themselves. And my advice to the agriculturists of this country is not to listen to sophistical arguments based upon the idea that the farmers are the best off people in Canada. I wish they were; I would like to see everybody well off. But eastern Canada has not yet quite understood how much sacrifice and toil has been needed to put the people of the western provinces in the position in which they are to-day. A man going into the western provinces-whether be went a few years ago, or whether he goes now-unless' he has ample capital, or unless he enjoys unusual good fortune, will spend fifteen years of hard work before he achieves a comfortable position. Manitoba and the older parts of Saskatchewan have gone through that fifteen years, and I admit that the farmers there are in fairly good circumstances. But evert the man going to the west to-day will need fifteen years to succeed, as I have said.
Now. I named the three classes of elevators, the line, the terminal and the transfer elevators. As to the terminal elevators, I believe our principal duty to-day lies with the elevators at Port Arthur and Fort Wil

liam. Before I get through I will read a report brought down by the government, which, I think, does not exactly agree with the remarks made by the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) the other day as to the quantity of wheat heretofore shipped out. I was surprised when I saw the government's figures showing how little wheat has passed through to the markets of Ontario or the markets of the world except through the terminal elevators at Port Arthur or Fort William. I have already said that we had been trying to solve problems connected with the line elevators. But, even if we solved those problems in the most successful manner, of what advantage would it be to us if the terminal elevators are left in the hands of people who treat the producers unfairly, who, in fact, for the last number of years-and the term is none too strong-have been stealing their wheat? (There is absolutely no question about it, because it has been proved by government officers). Then, I say, it is exceedingly important that we do something to remedy conditions in connection with these terminal elevators. The principal marketable product of the western farmer is wheat. The quality of our climate and soil is such that we have gained a reputation for producing the finest wheat in the world, and in such quantities that western Canada has been called ' The granary of the world.' But our wheat, on its way to the markets of the world, almost all passes through Fort William and Port Arthur.
Our farmers have known for years that our wheat was being manipulated in these terminal elevators. Formerly all our troubles were in connection with the line elevators, but now they have been increased in connection with these terminal elevators. The government have tried ways and means, and it may surprise this House to know that to-day this government is employing 95 men at Port Arthur and Fort William- what for? To handle this wheat? No, Sir, just to watch the other fellows that are stealing the wheat. They are there for no other reason. There is an absolute duplication of the men, the men who own the elevators and the men who are operating, and this government is paying $61,000 in employing 95 men to watch these other men, and who pays this $61,000? It all comes out of the grain growers; the wheat must pay all these men, there is no question about that. Now has there been any manipulation of wheat in Port Arthur and Fort William? We believe that it has been going on for years. When I brought this question up before, an amendment was moved from the other side of the House for delay, on the ground that the government was going to appoint men to supervise this work, and they did make appointments. At the very time of the instance I gave this after-1104
noon, there were some 75 men watching the operation of this mixing. Nevertheless this mixing is going on. I do not think that I am giving away any confidence when I say that I believe from information that the Department of Trade and Commerce is just as fully convinced as I am that it is going on, and they know that the only possible way we can protect the producer is that the man who operates the warehouse shall have no financial interest in the grain, and I think that can only be be accomplished by government operation.

The hon. gentleman speaks of information. Has he information which would lead this House to believe that during the present or past years' operation the Department of Trade and Commerce have any reason to believe that there has been manipulation at Fort William or Port Arthur?

Certainly, lots of information, and I will give it before I get through. It was done last year, according to a statement by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin) the other day. Now we may or we may not be in favour of government ownership and operation as a rule, I am not discussing that question to-day; but I do say that if there is any business in Canada to which the government operation is applicable, it is the handling of grain by these terminal elevators, and government operation can be applied to them with the least inconvenience of any industry I know of. Now, I will give my hon. friend the information for which he asks. I understand that to be in 1910.
I was referring to handling the crop of 1910, not to any action that was taken by the department, or to something that had occurred previously.

The last report is that of 1910, and this work was going on under the government system of having 75 men to watch the men who were doing this work. At present the number is 95, and I think it has been increased since. The information was supplied by the inspection department of Fort William and Port Arthur. The chief inspector, Mr. Gibbs, reports:
There were serious discrepancies in the returns of the terminal elevator companies' reports, as compared with those of the Inspection Department covering the same period.
This was on the 22nd of April, 1910. Mr. Castles went to Port Arthur, interviewed Mr. Gibbs, and returned to Winnipeg, and he says now:	'
At my request Inspector Gibbs made a formal complaint in writing, under oath, to enable me to hold an investigation under the provisions of the Manitoba Grain Act.

Now it would be very interesting to the House if I were to give a number of clauses from the Manitoba Grain Act, but I will not take up time by doing so.
The charges made in this case (as in the -other two cases) was that the company had [DOT]sent in incorrect and untrue statements.
The companies involved were the Canadian Pacific railway, the Consolidated Railway Company, the United Empire Company and the Port Arthur Company. They employed a lawyer by the name of Phillipps. Now I want to say that the grain dealers in Port Arthur and Fort William put every obstacle they could-this is Mr. Castles' own report-in the way of this investigation, and nearly all their [DOT]obstacles were met. But when it came to asking these men to produce their books, *and to allow them to be audited by the government officials, what did they do? Did they give up their books? No, Sir, they acknowledged the corn. They refused to give up their books, and admitted the charge Inspector Gibbs had made about the practice of the warehouse. Mr. Castles was correct, and these men were fined. The Port Arthur Company was fined in 1910, tout not nearly as much as they should have been fined, only $3,000; and the Consolidated Company were fined $50. The Empire Company $2,500. In all $5,550. I want to say with regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company that nothing could be found wrong with their handling of the grain, all that was wrong I believe were some technical errors. Eastern millers tell us that wheat that passes through Canadian Pacific Railway elevators is worth more for milling purposes than wheat of the same grade passing through privately owned and operated elevators. Mr. Castles and the government officials were convinced that there was nothing wrong, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was not fined. Now what is the inference? The Canadian Pacific railway had no interest in mixing the grain, in docking the grain; they were merely common carriers, and their only interest was to receive the grain and give it out again to the steamers, to be transported to the markets of the world. Now I think it is rather significant, and *goes to prove exactly what we believe, that the elevators must be controlled by men who have no financial interest in the wheat.
One of the chief troubles that we have had has been with what is called mixing grain. This was done in 1910. Some years ago the same system that has been carried on at Port Arthur and Fort William was in operation at Duluth and some of the men who were engaged in it at Dultlth are, I believe, those who have been carrying it on at Fort William and Port Arthur. The operation of mixing grain is carried *on in this way:	They buy a certain

amount of No. 1 Northern, No. 2 Northern, No. 3 Northern, and No. 4 Northern. The Manitoba Grain Act distinctly states that grain of different grades shall be plaeod in separate bins, that No. 1 shall be in one bin, No. 2 in another and No. 3 in another. But strange to say the same grades that go into the elevator do not come out. I ask the attention of the House to these figures. The shipments out of an elevator at Port Arthur of No. 1 Northern exceeded the receipts by 437,884 bushels. That is 437,884 bushels of wheat bought from the farmer for No. 2 Northern, or No. 3, or No.
4 and at the No. 2, 3, or 4 price was placed in a bin with No. 1 Northern and went out as No. 1 Northern, the dealer getting the benefit of the difference in price which sometimes amounts to as much as four cents a bushel. That affects us in a number of ways. I not only have to accept a No. 2 price for my wheat when I should get No. 1 price and I am, therefore, losing in that way, but it works out in another way. The No. 1 wheat that goes into the bin would average up. Some of it would be splendid wheat, some of it not so good, but the inspector at Winnipeg, where most of this wheat is inspected, calls it No. I. This wheat is shipped to Liverpool, and if wheat that would grade No. 3 and 4 is mixed with No. I the No. 1 grade is brought down to where it will just get through by the skin of its teeth; the whole of it is averaged up to a point where it will just grade No. 1 Northern. That goes over to the old country and the quality produced by the mixing operation reflects back on the prige that we get for our wheat at home. Everybody believes to-day that the value of our wheat is largely maintained by the Liverpool price. One of the complaints that our farmers make is that although we are supposed to produce the best wheat in the world because of our soil and climate, the grades are so deteriorated before the wheat reaches its market that the value is reflected back and the result is that the farmers receive a lower price.
Is the wheat all graded at Winnipeg?

The wheat is mostly all graded at Winnipeg. Sometimes when there is a rush on and the railway yards are full, wheat is permitted to be sent on to Port Arthur and is graded there, but you can say that as a matter of fact nearly all the wheat is graded at Winnipeg. We used to have this mixing going on at Winnipeg, but it is not going on to any great extent now because the government has remedied that part of the trouble. There used to be a mixing elevator at Winnipeg. They would run the wheat into this elevator and after mixing take out a carload of wheat which Mr. Horn, or his officers, would in-

spect. If it did not quite come up to the grade of No. 1 or No. 2 Northern they would ask Mr. Horn to allow them to take it back to the mixing elevator, they would treat it a little more and bring it up gradually to where it would grade No. 1 or No. 2 or No. 3 Northern. But a change has been made in that regard. Wheat that has been transhipped in Winnipeg is not graded until the bill of lading has been made
1	ut or until the wheat is ready to go to Fort William or Port Arthur. Therefore, I think I might say, replying to the question of the hon. leader of the opposition, that the grain is almost all graded at Winnipeg, and that no mixing goes on until the wheat reaches the terminal elevators. The process by which wheat is graded at Winnipeg is an interesting one. A car of wheat comes into Winnipeg from any part of the western provinces. It is the duty of the railway company to notify the inspector of the arrival of a car, the number and where it is placed in the yard. The wheat is sealed when it comes into Winnipeg. The inspector and his officsrs break the seal and gain access to the car. They have a long tube which they thrust into the wheat in a number of different places. It is a good deal like the instrument that dairymen use for testing cheese, with the exception that it is filled with a lot of little holes so that when they thrust the tube down into the wheat they are able to secure samples from the top to the bottom of the car. The sample is taken out, the car is resealed by these officers, it is sent on to Fort William or Port Arthur and then the result of the inspection of the sample, the inspectors having the number of the car, is sent to Inspector Gibbs, or to other persons at Port Arthur. As I said, 437,884 bushels of No. 1 Northern were shipped out more than were taken in. Where did they get the difference? That is by actual measurement by Inspector Gibbs. He also found 389,159 bushels of No.
2	Northern less in the elevator than were shipped in. The greater quantity of No. 1 was shipped out while there was a less quantity of No. 2 in the elevator than had been shipped in. Of No. 3 Northern, deducting shipments from receipts, there should have been on hand in the bins 155,975 bushels but when they came to measure up they only had 5,502 bushels, showing a discrepancy or shortage of 150,473 bushels. Deducting shipments from the receipts, there should have been on hand of No. 4 Northern 47,879 bushels, while there were only, by actual measurement, 4,001 bushels, the discrepancy being 43,869 bushels. That was going on under the supervision of seventy or eighty men in the employ of this government, and I am strongly of the opinion that it will go on in spite of all the Bills that this government may possibly be able to bring into
this House until the financial interest of the warehouseman is taken out of these elevators. In the Empire elevator the discrepancy is not quite as large, but they had the same difficulty. The officers at these elevators raised all sorts of objections. At last, when they were asked to produce their books in order to have an independent audit of them, they admitted at once that they had been doing wrong and refused to show their books.
Deducting shipments from receipts in this elevator, there should have been on hand on the 12th of December, 291,742 bushels, while there was only 175,000 bushels, or a discrepancy of 116,000. In No. 3 northern, deducting shipments from receipts there should have been on hand 346,000 bushels, but the examination showed only 166,000, or a shortage of 180,000; and so on. I think that should be very good proof of the kind of work that was going on. The railway terminal elevators were found to be conducted properly in connection with the Canadian Pacific railway, because there is no inducement for manipulation, and the warehousemen have no financial interest in the grain going through the elevator. Mr. Castles' report shows that the Port Arthur Elevator Company shipped out 169,066 more of No. 1 northern than they received. In the Empire elevator, Mr. Castles' report showed that the amount of No. 1 shipped out exceeded the receipts by 437,884 bushels, and that there was also a discrepancy or shortage, in No. 2 and No. 3 northern. In view of this condition of things, I maintain that the farmers of the west should be protected to a greater extent in the transport of their grain than ever they have been protected in the past.
I have referred to another evil in the grading of our wheat, and I shall not say more on that further than to remark that the farmer loses in two ways, because he does not get paid for his grain as he should be, and the quality of the wheat is depreciated in the British market. A few years ago most farmers in Manitoba and in some parts of Saskatchewan were absolutely compelled to sell their wheat because they had implements to pay for and had incurred debts during the summer and when the fall rush of wheat was on it was said there was a glut in the market and grain dealers recommended that they should spread the sale of their wheat over the different seasons of the year. The farmers became sufficiently well off to be able to adopt that system but they lacked grain room, and wheat cannot be shipped at any time of the year, because, for example, this winter the snow is so deep and the climate so severe that it would be absolutely impossible to haul wheat. Some of the farmers thought they would send their wheat to Port Arthur and Fort Wil-

liam, put it in the elevators but still retain control of it, so as to sell it when they wanted to. However, although they thought they were not putting their wheat upon the market and they would eventually receive a better price by distributing its sale over different months of the year, they found their wheat was still going forward and that was one of the complaints against the Consolidated Elevator Company. The wheat that the farmers thought they were holding was being loaned and sent forward, and at the same time although they were doing this they were charging the farmer for the storage of this wheat all the time. These are facts that cannot be disputed. Another evil-and goodness knows I have already detailed enough to convince any government that one of the greatest Canadian industries should be better protected-another evil is that when the wheat is inspected at Winnipeg the inspector sends a certificate to Port Arthur that the wheat is of a certain grade with a certain percentage of dockage, which means that at Port Arthur and Fort William it should be cleaned of the 2, 3 or 5 per cent dockage, as the case may be, and then sent on. After the farmer had paid the freight on this dirty grain down to Port Arthur and Fort William, the elevators always had the privilege of using the dockage for their own purposes. But what did they do? If it was only about 2 per cent dockage, they allowed the wheat to go on without treating it at all, and when it arrived in the British market without being cleaned that reflected back again upon the quality of our wheat. The four principles for which the farmers of the west contend are: that there should not be mixing, that there should not be unfair dockage, that wheat should not be loaned, and that wheat should be cleaned at the terminal elevators, according to the certificate of the wheat inspector at Winnipeg. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of that western country are obliged to conform to the Grain Act to the letter, and if the farmers are compelled to keep to the strict letter of the law, my duty here to-day is to see that the grain dealer is dealt with in the same way. I am, however, of the opinion that no amount of supervision or inspection can eventually prevent manipulation in our terminals so long as they are owned and operated by private interests. In taking that stand I am reiterating the sentiment expressed by the hon. gentleman from Regina (Mr. Martin) when he spoke on this subject the other day. I am glad the hon. gentleman (Mr. Martin) spoke as he did on this matter; I am not dealing with this question from any political partisan point of view; I believe we have suffered tremendously in that western country for want of proper Mr. SCHAFFNER.
supervision and because our grain has been manipulated by the grain dealer, and I think Liberals and Conservatives alike should endeavour to seek a remedy. The House may remember that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Martin) moved an amendment to the motion, that I moved in this House, and with that I find no fault. A few years ago Mr. Martin's amendment was to the effect that the system adopted then by government should have a trial.
Mr. Martin now says:
The system has now been given a fair trial with the result that it has proved itself absolutely inadequate to meet the situation.
He also says on page 2445 of ' Hansard
I have gradually come to the conclusion that we will never be protected properly in the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur until we have these elevators owned and operated by the government.
There could not be anything more pronounced than that, and I am thoroughly in sympathy with the remarks of the hon. gentleman. Now, Mr. Speaker, what I have referred to to-day all took place under a system of supervision which the government supposed would solve the problem. At that time there were 70 men in the employ of the government inspecting the terminal elevators, but the manipulation continued under their very eyes and they were powerless to prevent it. I say that it is an absolute impossibility to exercise such supervision as will prevent the mixing of the grain, even if you have 500 men there. These elevator people have belts running from one elevator to another, and from one bin to another, and what is to prevent them going in there at night and transferring grain from one bin to another ? How is any supervision going to prevent that ? And this manipulation and stealing of wheat has been going on for years. I believe I am not out of the way when I say that the farmers of the west have lost at least ten millions of dollars in the value of the wheat that has been taken from them by the operation of these privately-owned elevators. The farmers were here a short time ago to bring several matters before the government of the day. There was the reduction of the tariff, the Hudson Bay railway, the chilled meat question; last, but by no means least, the terminal elevator question. This question is as important to the east as to the west, because the more money the farmers receive, the more money Montreal, Toronto and every eastern manufacturing interest is going to get. I said at the beginning that there might be some difference of opinion on this subject; but three years ago the farmers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, stood almost to a man for government ownership of these

elevators. With regard to line elevators, they have to some extent, changed their opinion; but with regard to terminal elevators, I think I can fairly say that they are practically a unit to-day in favour of government ownership and operation. The trouble is not in the ownership of the elevators, but in their operation. This wheat question is becoming a big question, and we have only touched the fringe of it. It is estimated that there are in the three prairie provinces 171,000,000 acres that will produce wheat, and we have under cultivation to-day not more than 13,000,000 or 14,000,000 acres. The hon. member for Regina told us the other day that Saskatchewan alone produced last year 90,000,000 bushels. The other day I placed on the Order Paper some questions, which, with the answers to them, I think are worthy of a place in ' Hansard ' to give this House some idea of the magnitude of this subject. Out of three years' crops, all the wlmat which did not pass through the terminal elevators at Port Arthur and Fort William amounted to but 5,200,000 bushels. This shows that the question as to the best way to operate and control these elevators at Port Arthur and Fort William is on; that might well engage our attention. I am not a prophet or the son of a prophet, and consequently may be wrong. The Bill which the government is going to bring down, no doubt, in the opinion of the government, meets ths demand, but I do not believe it. I believe that there is only one remedy, and that is to take the operation of these elevators out of the hands of the men who -have a financial interest in them. I .repeat, Mr. Speaker, no amount of supervision or inspection can effectually prevent manipulation in our terminals so long as they are owned and operated by private interests, which can be benefited thereby. Our farmers in the past have been divided, through lack of organization they have failed to accomplish much, but they have started organizing. They have followed the example of the railways, and the manufacturers, and by .means of organization intend to make their influence felt. To-day the ship of these farmers is afloat, it is controlled by competent officers and manned by able seamen, and the port to which it is making is the port of the greatest good to the greatest number.
Can the hon. gentleman inform the Housi to what extent the farmers of Manitoba have taken advantage of the government owned elevators during the past season?

My hon. friend will understand that the government operation of these elevators in Manitoba is a very new thing; at least half the crop was shipped before the government took charge of the elevators either by purchase or building. Further, for years there has not been such a small quantity of wheat to ship from southern Manitoba as this year. But the commissioner, who was the chairman of the organization which met in this room, told me that he believed the new system was going to work out splendidly. Furthermore, the farmers of Manitoba must be coming to that opinion because 90 per cent of the points at which elevators are located have petitioned the government to either buy or Mr. SCHAFFNER,
build and operate the elevators at those points.

As a similar resolution to the one before us was offered for our consideration a couple of weeks ago, I do not propose to discuss this matter at any length to-day. I only rise to say that, in view of the fact that the government have introduced into the Senate a Bill dealing with this whole subject, we might very well postpone discussion until we have this Bill before us. I am as strongly in earnest about getting a satisfactory solution of the grain difficulties in the west as my hon. friend can possibly be. I might say that, notwithstanding the very strong criticism he makes of the present method of government supervision and inspection, there are one or two points which he has overlooked, and to which I would call his attention.
In the first place, government supervision was carried on to a very limited extent-[DOT] that is, the staff was a very limited one until two years ago. And while it is true that certain terminal elevators, so far as the handling of the grain crop of 1909 is concerned, were brought to book last year, it is also true that they were brought to book by the very method of supervision which my hon. friend condemned. These offences would not have been discovered and those guilty of them would not have been penalized had it not been for the supervision that is being carried on by the officers of the government. I asked my hon. friend if he were aware of any similar transaction^, in handling the grain crop of 1910. He did not give me an answer to that question. If this government supervision is absolutely valueless, as my hon. friend alleges it is, he ought to explain how it comes that it was by this very supervision that these transgressors were brought to book. I might also point out that my hon. friend has not taken cognizance of the fact that since the crop of 1909 was handled, further steps have been taken to protect the interests of the farmer who ships his grain to Fort William or Port Arthur by the appointment of the registration bureau to which I referred some days ago. The trouble in the past has been that the penalties have not been sufficiently severe. If the operation of mixing were carried on to any very large extent, the elevator interest could afford to pay a very considerable fine and still be very largely the gainer. However, I said in opening that it is not my intention to deal with this question to any extent to-day; because, while I take the position that my hon. friend may be correct and that ultimately it may be necessary to establish government ownership and operation of the terminal and transfer elevators, yet I hold that that fact has not yet been absolutely de-

monstrated. And I reiterate the position I took the other day, that until this is absolutely demonstrated such action as is proposed by my hon. friend is premature and might be dangerous even to the grain trade itself.
And, in view of the fact that the government have a Bill which will presently be before this House, in which, I understand, provision is made of a final remedy for the very thing my hon. friend proposes to meet by means of government ownership and operation, a Bill which, I understand, provides for a commission such as I suggested when discussing this question a couple of weeks ago, and gives the commission the very widest powers possible in dealing with this trade, giving them the same control of the grain situation in Canada as the warehouse and grain commission has in the State of Minnesota, where, I believe, the grain laws are probably more satisfactory than in any other part of North America-I say, in view of these facts, it would be unwise for this House to lay down finally and absolutely the principle proposed in the motion of my hon. friend until we have had some opportunity of seeing for ourselves, of investigating, of thinking over and discussing this measure which the government proposes to bring before the House within the next few days.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Neely) will permit me, I would like to ask a question. Does he believe, so far as he has information of the Bill, that it will provide for the government operation of these elevators? In other words, will it take the operation oi these elevatorj out of the hands of the grain dealers?

I am free to say that, until to-day, I have been quite as much in the dark concerning the provisions of this Bill as my hon. friend. I had no opportunity to see the Bill and consider its- clauses. But, when this question came up to-day, I took the trouble to send to the distribution office and procure a copy of the Bill, and I believe my hon. friend could procure a copy in the same way. And I do find a provision which, if it is not out of order, I would like to read:
The Governor in Council may authorize the minister to construct, acquire, lease or expropriate for His Majesty any terminal elevator if parliament has granted the money for such purpose.
The Expropriation Act shall, in any case, apply to the leasing and acquisition of such terminal elevator and to the ascertaining of the compensation to he paid therefor.
That is as much information as I can give my hon. friend, because I have not had time even to look through the other provisions of the Bill except in a casual wav.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman a question if it would not be interrupting him too much. I understand him to say that government ownership might ultimately be necessary, but that this had not yet been demonstrated to the satisfaction of the House. Does he say that the case presented by the farmers' delegation from the west is not sufficient demonstration of this point to satisfy parliament that it was absolutely necessary?

While it was demonstrated, not only by the farmers1, but by the prosecution made by the officers of the government that, so far as the handling of the crops of 1909 and preceding years is concerned, there probably was manipulation of the grain at Port Arthur and Fort William, and while the farmers demonstrated that a remedy was necessary, they only gave it as their opinion that the one method of reform was government ownership and operation. I can hardly go so far as to say that they did demonstrate the absolute necessity of government ownership and operation; they gave it as their opinion. But farmers' opinions change like other peoples. I notice that a large body of the Grain Growers of Saskatchewan, in convention assembled, have unanimously adopted a co-operative scheme in connection with the operation of interior elevators-line elevators-whereas, some years ago, as my hon. friend (Mr. Schaffner) has very truly said, the only remedy favoured by many of the farmers of Saskatchewan seemed to be government operation. The same change might occur in this case. But the point I am making is that, in any case, whether government operation be necessary as a final remedy or not, a commission must be appointed

that is, if the government so decide to take over these elevators, there must be a commission to operate them, some body in which shall be vested power to deal with the whole grain trade throughout the length and breadth of Canada. These must be men able to become thoroughly versed in the conditions of the grain trade-in fact the probability is that they will be men who are well versed in that business; they certainly should be men who know a good deal of the grain trade. If these gentlemen, after they have been in office for a reasonable length of time, come' to the conclusion that they cannot stop evils in any other way than by government operation, and if they make report to that effect, I am convinced that the government will not hesitate a single moment in putting into effect the recommendation of this commission. That is my answer to my hon. friend's question, and that is the position I take on this whole matter. Now, Sir, in view of the fact that I hold these sentiments, in view of the fact, as I have said, that the government

have this Bill introduced in the Senate, and that it is presently to be brought before this House, I beg to move :
That all words after ' that ' in this resolution be struck out, and the following be substituted-
Inasmuch as a Bill has been introduced by the government and is now pending in the Senate, dealing with the present system of operating the terminal elevators, it is not expedient to proceed with this question in advance of the consideration of the said Bill by this House.

Allow me, in the first place, to congratulate the hen. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) on the able and thorough way in which he has dealt with this important question, and also on the w'ay he has stuck to his point, a point that I think is endorsed by all the members from the northwest, and by all the men raising grain in that country, namely, the absolute necessity of government operation of the terminal elevators. I have already placed myself on record as saying that, in my opinion, nothing short of government operation will remove the evil under which the people of the northwest are suffering in regard to the handling of their grain at Fort William and Port Arthur. I have taken the position, which I think is a logical one, that once the government have assumed the responsibility of granting a certificate that grain is of a certain quality as No. 1 Northern, No. 2 Northern and No. 3 Northern, it should take such measures as will absolutely ensure that that grain reaches the consumer in the same condition in which it has passed from the hands of the grain growers, and that there should be no sort of tampering with it. Two years ago the members from the northwest, on the other side of the House, blocked a resolution which was introduced by my hon. friend from Souris, asking for government operation of terminal elevators. They proposed that an opportunity should be given for a fuller method of government inspection of those elevators. That system has been tried, and it has been found wanting. A few months ago the country was startled to learn that frauds had been perpetrated under the very noses of the inspectors. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Neely) has taken a good deal of credit for the government inspectors from the fact that it was they who called attention to the frauds. Now, it seems to me as rather singular that credit should be given to men who subsequently discovered a fraud which had actually taken place under their very noses, and which it was their special duty to prevent. The hon. gentleman went on to state that no charges of fraud could be substantiated at the present time in regard to -the handling of the grain crop of last year. I think, if my memory is right, Mr. NEELY.
that at the very time the grain growlers' deputation was being received at Ottawa, a statement was made that such charges would be again preferred in regard to the handling of the grain crop of last year. Any w'ay, let me point out that, although frauds took place at a very early .stage in the handling of the crop of 1909, it was not, I think until April, 1910, that the matter reached a point v/here a prosecution could he entered in connection with those frauds. This is the svstem of government inspection that has been proved a failure up to the present time. The government now' propose to introduce another experiment in the way of still further government control and inspection. Unfortunately, I have not been able to get hold of a copy of the Bill with which the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) seems to have been favoured. I went into the distribution office on Saturday afternoon, and they hnd not got the Bill at that time.

1 have a correction to make. The Minister of the Interior sent up to the distribution bureau a short time rgo for a copy of the Bill. I was under the impression that the Bills were in the distribution office, and I have just discovered that the copy he handed to me was his own private copy, and that he was not able to get one at the distribution office.

I have just sent up a written request to the distribution office for a copy of the Bill, and they send me word that they have not got it yet. So members on the other side of the House have an opportunity of studying the details of this measure, which gentlemen on this side of the House have not. During the debate which took place a few weeks ago I noticed hon. gentlemen opposite referring to some _ details of this measure; so w7e were certainly at a disadvantage in discussing the course which w'e understood was to be pursued when this Bill was biought in. Now', with regard to fuller inspection at Fort William and Port Arthur, my hon. friend from Souris has stated that it is absolutely impossible to have thorough and complete control of the grain which passes through these elevators. I confess that I had begun to think there must be something wrong, when there was a body of 75 to 90 inspectors at w'ork there last year, and this year again, who had not been able to control the grain passing through those elevators; that seemed to me extraordinary. I w'as under the impression that the government were making appointments of men to act at those places as they were doing in other cases throughout the country, leaving the nomination in the hands of the Liberal committee at Fort William and Port Arthur, and W'ere making appointments of inspectors at these places from the recommendations of the Literal committee. If

that is the case, it only shows that the men thus appointed- were not able to carry on the work which was entrusted to them, end it is another instance of the mischievous nature of the patronage system to which this government has absolutely surrendered itself since it has been in power.
When the Grain Growers deputation were down here in December last they were quite definite as to what they wanted with respect to this matter. Not only were they definite but they had grain dealers and millers with them who also gave evidence to the effect that the government operation of terminal elevators was the only thing which would satisfactorily control the passage of wheat through these elevators, and prevent any fraud in connection with it. They made out a remarkably complete case and I have heard practically nothing said by any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House to show that the stand taken by the grain growers at that time is not an absolutely sound one. In addition to that let me put in the evidence of a resolution that was unanimously passed by the legislative assembly of the province of Saskatchewan at the last session of the House, to this effect:
Whereas, this House is of the opinion that under existing conditions, both interior and terminal elevators being private and identical interests operate to the disadvantage of the grain growers of Saskatchewan;
Therefore, be it resolved, that in the opinion of this House the government of Canada should own and operate the terminal elevators.
This resolution was unanimously passed by the legislature of Saskatchewan at the last session, affording an additional argument why, in the opinion of men well fitted to judge with regard to this matter, government operation alone will meet the exigencies of the case.
I might point out also to the Prime Minister and to the hon. gentlemen who sit on that side of the House, the additional necessity at the present time that grain, which is going by the Canadian route, and which receives a Canadian certificate, should be absolutely above suspicion, and that the certificate should be absolutely reliable. It lies in the reciprocity negotia-tiations which have been carried on during the last few weeks. If the certificate of our government can be absolutely relied upon by the consumers in Great Britain as giving the correct quality of the grain, I have no doubt in the world that our grain will once again command the very high value which it used to command on the Liverpool markets and which it has not been commanding of late years. The statement was made by gentlemen who were down here representing the Manitoba Grain Growers' Association just about a year ago, that for several months on the British market Manitoba wheat had been at a lower value than many other wheats upon that market. This is the statement which was [DOT]made by them in a letter which they addressed to the government at that time:
Due to its own high quality for making baker's flour, Manitoba No. 1 Northern usually brings a premium over all other wheats in Britain, yet from early in October to December, 1909, ' Manitoba ' was the lowest priced wheat in the Liverpool market excepting some United States wheat.
If that condition continues to exist then we shall see, if the reciprocity arrangement is carried out, our wheat going out through the United States, and not through the elevators at Port Arthur and Fort William. That is a condition that I am sure we all most earnestly wish to avoid, and for that reason in itself I would urge that the government undertake the operation of these elevators and see, when they give a a certificate of quality, that that certificate is valid when the grain reaches the markets of the world. I only hope that in addition to the government undertaking the operation of the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur for the reasons I have stated they would hurry up the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. That will give us another and a far better route to the markets of the world than we have at the present time, and it will also assist in preventing our wheat from being carried to these markets by the American route.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has, on behalf of the government, introduced a Bill in the Senate, dealing with this matter, it will not be necessary for me to-night, speaking on this motion, to anticipate the discussion which will ensue in this House when that Bill comes before us. There is, of course, no doubt that a great many irregularities have occurred at the terminal elevators, and the only question of difference between us is, or should be, as to what is the best remedy to provide for the prevention of these irregularities. When the grain growers from the west were here in December last, there was a conference between them and members of the government as to the measures which should be taken to regulate the terminal elevators, and as I understand it, the proposals then made by the government were satisfactory to the delegates. When I was home during the Christmas holidays, I found the idea prevalent among the farmers, that

they would be satisfied with the government measure which they were led to believe would be introduced and which has since been presented to parliament. One of the provisions of that Bill is that there should be a commission appointed to oversee the business of the elevators, to get a perfect knowledge concerning the conduct of that business, and, if the business were not conducted in the interests of the grain growers that this commission should make recommendations to the government as to the taking over of these elevators and the provision of a parliamentary grant for that purpose. When that Bill comes before us, as I say, it will then be time enough for us to consider whether it is calculated to _ mitigate the evils which undoubtedly exist, and anything we may say to-night would be unnecessarily anticipatory of that discussion. Of course, we know that when a great many bushels of grain go through these elevators, a very small margin on each bushel would amount to a good many dollars in the pockets of the men operating the elevators, and so we must suppose that those guilty of manipulation, have very good reason for urging that conditions should remain as they are at present. However, I believe the legislation introduced by the government, will put an end to wrong-doing in that respect. As we all know, government ownership has not proved a huge success in this country. Our experience with the Intercolonial railway teaches us that, and our experience with that railway also teaches us that since it has been placed under a commission, its operation has been fairly satisfactory. In view of the fact that we will have to consider this question on the government Bill, I think it is only fair that the hon. member from Souris should withdraw his resolution, which at the present time I deem to be inexpedient. I have great pleasure in seconding the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely).

The question of the terminal elevators is a most important one to the grain growers of western Canada, and I congratulate the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner), that he has brought it to the attention of the House at the present time. I congratulate him also on his able presentation of the case for the western farmers, and upon the fact that he has been able to submit to us so many illuminating facts in connection with the question. This government has known for years that the grain growers of the west have been continuously robbed at the terminal elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur. I well remember attending a meeting in the West Block during the session of 1908-9 when the grain grow-Mr. CASH.
ers and millers of eastern Canada and the grain growers of western Canada appeared before Sir Richard Cartwright and placed before him all the facts which would convince any reasonable man that the grain growers were being continually robbed and deprived of the just reward of their labours. It was shown to the Minister of Trade and Commerce then, that profits which were theirs were filched from them and handed over to whom ? Not to Canadians-because with the exception of the Canadian Pacific Railway elevators, the elevators at Port Arthur and Fort William are controlled by American citizens-but to men who come from a foreign land. For years has the government known that this state of affairs existed, but in this case, as in a great many others, they refused to interfere, for the benefit of our own citizens, and allowed these people to continue robbing the hard working people of Canada. The hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner), has dealt with this matter so fully, that it is unnecessary for me to do further than endorse the sentiments expressed by him. I trust, that even though the Bill presented by the government does not give us government ownership, it will to some extent remove the grievances which during the past few years we have suffered in western Canada.

As a farmer, and as the representative of a farming constituency, it is most gratifying to me to find my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner), and his friends so anxious to meet demands of the western grain growers. Their attitude in this respect, makes me very- hopeful that we shall have an early collapse of the reciprocity debate, because, if the hon. member from Souris, and his friends will canvass the western farmers, I am sure they will find a large majority of them in favour of this particular method of getting larger markets for their produce. Having no desire to impugn the honest sincerity of my hon. friend (Mr. Schaffner), and his friends in their express desire to find new markets for the farmers, and especially to meet their demands and wishes, I repeat that I am extremely hopeful they will see their way to support that great measure of reciprocity which has been presented by the government for our consideration.
Nothing could possibly give me greater amazement than to see the light-hearted manner in which it would appear that a party calling itself Conservative is prepared to take up a great scheme of state socialism. I am aware that so great a thinker as Sir William Harcourt in the field of politics once said: ' We are all socialists now,' and in a limited sense there is some truth in that statement. But Conservat-

ism, as I have always understood it, is in its very nature opposed to socialism. There seemed to be some glimmering of that thought in the mind of my hon. friend from Souris when he calmly informed this House that he had no desire to discuss the question of state ownership. But the question as he puts it is a question of state ownership, and in that sense it is nothing but rank, pure, simple unadulterated socialism. Socialism is defined by its leading advocates on both sides of the Atlantic as ' government ownership and operation of the means of producing and distributing wealth.' The elevators are a great means of the distribution of wealth, and our hon. friends opposite propose, before other expedients have been exhausted, light-heartedly to commit the government and the parliament and the people of Canada to this very large and serious instalment of state socialism. Well, I cannot understand their attitude upon that question. In debating this matter with socialists themselves, I have pointed out that in their criticisms of government they stand in the same position as all opposition parties in this country. They are continually saying in plain language what the opposition here is continually saying, and what Liberal oppositions in provincial legislatures in this country are continually saying, that they are none too sure of the uprightness with which governments today are handling public funds, public departments and public affairs generally. Now, where is the logic-I would like to put this to my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake), who had a good, old-fashioned education in his youth-where is the logic of continually basing opposition to governments as they exist upon their alleged incompetence to handle business matters, and asking this House to commit itself to an indefinite extension of the field of government operation? I cannot see the logic of. it; and, to be truthful, Sir, I am very frightened at such an extension of the field of government operation. I believe that as a rule a man will do better work for himself than he will get done by a partner; I believe an individual field of operation is better than a partnership; I believe a partnership is better than a company in handling business affairs; and I believe the worst thing in the world to handle business affairs is a government, and the more its operations are restricted to the proper functions of a government the better it will be for the country.
To put it plainly, what our hon. friends want to do is to put a stop to thieving. They allege that there is absolute thieving going on in connection with the handling of grain. They call it manipulation. Well, that term would be a very good periphrasis for an act of burglary, but I do not think the moral quality of manipulation in this
instance is very different from that of thieving. I have always thought that the proper way to deal with thieves was by the criminal law, and one of the reasons for delay in this particular instance is that in the measure of inspection which the government at present has in its hands you have a means which has proved to be so far efficient that some of the thieving has been detected, and punishment has been meted out to the culprits. I want to put it to my friends fairly: is it not likely that if we increase our vigilance, if we improve our machinery, we may still be able under the criminal law to put down this thing without committing ourselves to a great scheme of state socialism?
There are other reasons for hesitation in this matter which I would like to impress upon our hon. friends opposite. The very last debate in this House, followed by a division upon a farming question, so far as I remember, was just before the Christmas adjournment, on the question of establishing a government system of handling chilled meat; and our hon. friends opposite were at that time perfectly prepared to encourage the government of this country to embark upon a huge system of government interference in the chilled meat industry. But what do we find to-day?- and I draw the particular attention of my hon. friend from Souris to this point. We find that some of the very men who were making these demands, which he is so solicitous to meet in the exact way in which they were presented, are saying that so large a market will be obtained for the meat producers of the west under the proposed scheme of reciprocity that there will be no need for this chilled meat project.
I was very much impressed with the excellent speech of my hon. friend from Hum-bolt (Mr. Neely) on this question, in the debate on the resolution of my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin). One of the points that he made was that we are just at the beginning of our wheat production in tne west. I have mentioned in this House before the fact that we have in /the three prairie provinces 300,000,000 acres of splendid arable land. We have not to-day under cultivation 20,000,000 acres. If the government were to embark on such a course as has been suggested, no man could see the end of it. You would be indefinitely enlarging the field of government interference in a matter which is much better handled by private enterprise, with a strict and rigid enforcement of the criminal law.
In all these considerations there appears to me to be very good ground for giving pause to hon. gentlemen opposite, for taking time to consider this question, and especially to consider a measure which is to be almost immediately presented to the Senate for the more efficient handling of elevators under that scheme of individual-

ism which after all is the outstanding quality of the race which upholds this Empire, and which is the only quality the exercise of which can in the end build up a strong people and a strong nation. On these grounds I shall vote without hesitation against the motion of my hon. friend from Souris at this time, and shall wait with some degree of confidence for the production of the government measure on the subject.

Mr. Speaker, it is always interesting to hear the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. He has a very refreshing manner of dealing with things, and certainly a manner entirely his own. He is greatly concerned with the attitude of hon. gentlemen on this side, and would be exceedingly glad if he could recruit some supporters for the government on the question of reciprocity, which appears to he a kind of nightmare for him as it is for some members of the cabinet as well.
The hon. gentleman talks of socialism.
I do not know whether he speaks as an expert or not, but he is very much alarmed over the name of -state socialism. Let me say that I care .not what nam; you give this -proposition, if it is in the interests of the country and particularly of the farmers of the west, who more than any other class are making Canada great, I shall support it as a good measure. We are told that the government have introduced a Bill in the Senate under the sponsorship of Sir Richard Cartwright. Well, we have not yet seen that Bill, although this House has been in session three months and this question is one of the greatest importance to the most important class in the community. Is not this really an attempt to sidetrack the farmers when we know that this Bill of which the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) speaks does not touch the question before the House? The steps which the government have taken -so far, having proved utterly inefficient as the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin) demonstrated the other day, the government should not put the farmers off with promises any longer but do something -practical. What is this measure, which has -been introduced in the Senate aft;r this long delay, going to do? It is simply going to give us a little more of what we have too much of already. It proposes to establish another court. The Lord knows we have quite enough courts in Canada as it is. It is not courts w? want -but justice. It is not a multiplication of officers, but efficient work that we require ; and to tell us that the government are going to establish another tribunal similar to the railway board, is simply to tell us that this wrong-doing is to get on just as before, and Mr. CLARK.
that when any offence is committed the offender may be brought before this court and punished. What we want, however, is not punishment but a remedy. A commission would b? all right but not such a commission as the government proposes. What is required is a commission to operate the elevators, to do justice in th.e first instance, and put a stop to the thieving, which my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) so much deplores. My hon. friend speaks of Conservatism as he understands it. Why, he never did understand _ it. In that respect he is not very much different from many hon. gentlemen on that side, they are so wedded to their idols, although often elected as- independents. I do not know whether my hon. friend got in as an independent but I would almost think he did, to judge by his intense partisanship, because I notice there is no man so utterly subservient as the so-called independent. I see my hon. friend dissents from this suggestion of independence. He is worried about our being light-hearted. Well, every man is light-hearted when he knows he is doing what is right, but when a man knows he has to come forward in response to the party whip to do the government's bidding, if he has any conscience at all-and a few of those gentleman have -he can not possibly be light-hearted, he is despondent as my hon. friend certainly is on this occasion.
My -hon. friend -asks where is the logic of constantly condemning the government, and then asking the government to undertake additional work. If they are inefficient and incompetent, why should we ask them to do more? My hon. friend does not understand the situation. Those -men opposite are not going to be at the head of affairs forever. What we want is to get good laws, and then a good government ; but I admit that if I thought those hon. gentlemen were going to be in power much longer, I would hesitate committing anything to them.
